newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: High Asia jet fuel prices trigger Med shipments.
newsitem.headline: High Asia jet fuel prices trigger Med shipments.

text.p: Firm Asian jet fuel prices, which have spurred shipments from the Mediterranean and regional refiners to raise output, could lead to softer prices as demand is not strong enough, traders said on Tuesday.
"On paper, the number works for arbitrage cargoes to come to Asia with the spread seen at $28-$29 per tonne between the Mediterranean and Asia" a trader with a Japanese company said.
"But the (sales) outlet would be questionable."
Traders said two Mediterranean jet fuel cargoes are being fixed by a European major and a Swiss trader for arrival in end-July/early August to Asia.
Since last week, refiners in Singapore have also started to optimise the production of jet-kerosene fuel because of the current wide price differential (spread) of jet over gas oil.
This would mean that they could raise jet fuel output by 10-20 percent, a refiner said.
Physical spot jet fuel cargoes are now about $2.50 per barrel above gas oil values, while the swaps spread between the two products for July are $1.95/$2.10.
Most traders said jet fuel is overpriced as there is no real demand from the region other than Indonesia.

They said that even Indonesian demand, estimated at two million barrels in July and about the same volume for August, has been easily covered by its term contract with Kuwait and from majors and traders in Singapore.
Traditional buyers, South Korea and Japan, were also not expected to seek incremental jet-kerosene cargoes.
Traders said fixed price jet, offered at $24.60 per barrel for prompt cargoes, is the current ceiling and prices should be falling from now on as buyers are currently sidelined.
They said jet fuel started to climb over gas oil over the past three weeks when it reached a 20-month low of under $23.00 per barrel.
The rally was triggered by a group of Singapore traders and a Japanese trader who bought at $22.40 per barrel for end-June and $23.50 for early July lifting cargoes, free-on-board basis.
Prices hit $24.65 last Thursday when the Singapore trader bought a mid-July cargo from a European major.
Traders said with the arbitrage being wide open and refiners maximising jet production, the current price level could only find support if the local trader continued to buy at current levels.

But signs of a crack in jet values were already being seen on Tuesday. The swaps jet/gas oil spread has started to slip by 5-10 cents from Monday for July, while the spread for August has fallen by 20-25 cents from Monday to $1.55/$1.75.
Traders also noted that prices in forward months were lower than the prompt month, which indicated that long term demand is not strong, while the prompt market might have been artificially supported.
But traders said if jet fuel values continued to take a beating, Asian refiners could easily switch back to producing more gas oil at the expense of jet.
This, as well as the closing of the arbitrage window when jet prices fall, could provide some support to the ailing jet market.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3084)
